source.text: Dross is the molten metal that solidifies on the workpiece. Some amount of dross is always present when cutting with air plasma. However, you can control the amount and type of dross by adjusting your system correctly for your application.

High-speed dross forms when the cutting speed is too fast and the arc lags behind. It forms as a thin, linear bead of solid metal attached very close to the cut. It forms to the bottom of the cut and is often more difficult to remove. Decrease your speed to reduce this type of dross.

 Dross is more likely to form on warm or hot metal than on cool metal. For example, the first cut in a series of cuts is likely to produce the least dross. As the workpiece heats up, more dross may form on subsequent cuts.

proposal: 1. Symptom 'Dross on the workpiece' -> MAY_INDICATE -> FailureMode 'Cut speed is too fast, causing the arc to lag behind'. Meaning: The symptom may indicate the specified failure mode. Conditions: Cutting speed is too fast; arc lags behind.

2. Symptom 'Dross on the workpiece' -> MAY_INDICATE -> FailureMode 'Workpiece is warm or hot'. Meaning: The symptom may indicate the specified failure mode. Conditions: More likely on warm or hot metal than cool metal.

source.text: TABLE COLUMNS: Problem | Possible causes | Possible solutions

Problem: The circuit breaker trips frequently while you are cutting. | Possible causes: • The amperage adjustment knob is set too high for the input circuit. • The wrong consumables are being used. • The input circuit is not delivering sufficient power to the power supply. • The operator is stretching the arc by holding the torch too far from the workpiece when cutting. • The extension cord is too long, is damaged, or is not capable of delivering sufficient power to the power supply. | Possible solutions: • Turn down the cutting current. See Step 3 – Adjust the output current on page 47. • Make sure the correct consumables are installed for this power supply and torch. See Consumable use on page 37. • Operate the system on a 240 VAC input circuit whenever possible. • Avoid stretching the arc. Drag the torch on the workpiece. See Edge start on a workpiece on page 54. • Operate the system without using an extension cord. If you must use an extension cord, use a heavy conductor cord of the shortest possible length. See Extension cord recommendations on page 33. • Make sure nothing else is drawing power on the same circuit.

answers.text: Keep statements 1 and 2. Statements 3–5 are not supported by the excerpts provided.
answers.rationale: The manual prescribes the J3 VBUS check and says that absent VBUS after disconnecting J2 leads to checking the power board; the compressor-enable and J1/J9 wire checks in statements 3–5 are not shown.

answers.text: Keep statements 1 and 2; statement 3 is not supported because the manual says to replace the torch body if the plunger does not move freely, not that the failure mode affects the torch body.
answers.rationale: The manual prescribes checking whether the plunger moves freely and replacing the torch lead when it moves freely after the low-resistance finding; it directs torch-body replacement when the plunger does not move freely, but does not state an AFFECTS relation.

answers.text: Keep statements 1 and 2. The excerpts place the hose-seating check in the test for low air pressure affecting performance, and prescribe the gauge reading during a test cut; they do not support the drain-hose claim in statement 3.
answers.rationale: The manual checks whether the gas-supply hoses are fully seated as part of investigating low air pressure and specifies the test-cut gauge check, but it does not say a gas-line leak affects a drain hose.

The manual separately describes visual signs on the power board and how to isolate a problem when resistance values indicate one; it does not link that isolation procedure to the listed visual failure mode.

answers.text: The manual says to look for broken or loose wiring connections, burn or char marks, and damaged components during the visual inspection. It directs the reader to the troubleshooting guide only when the visual inspection and initial resistance check find no problems and the power supply still does not operate correctly; it does not link that referral to the listed defects.
answers.rationale: The proposal joins the visual-inspection findings on page 61 to a referral that page 63 prescribes only when those checks find no problems.

answers.text: The excerpts prescribe measuring W-to-B and R-to-B, but do not state that the readings should be compared to diagnose unequal readings; only the W-to-B expected value is given.

answers.text: For a broken wire in the torch lead, replace the faulty torch lead; replacing the cap-sensor switch applies only when that switch is faulty.
answers.rationale: The manual says to replace whichever part is faulty, so a broken torch-lead wire supports replacing the lead, not the cap-sensor switch as an alternative.

answers.text: The flowchart directs disconnecting J2 and rechecking LED D5 when LED D5 is not on initially, not when it is on.
